newsitem.title: USA: Denial of NYSEG rate increases recommended.
newsitem.headline: Denial of NYSEG rate increases recommended.

text.p: The staff of the New York Public Service Commission has recommended that New York State Electric & Gas Corp be denied two rate increases of $45 million per year called for in the second and third years of its 1995 rate case.
The staff's initial brief in the utility's restructuring case also calls for denial of stranded cost recovery unless NYSEG agrees to divest its generation assets.
The brief also seeks swift initial unbundling of NYSEG's tariffs to help prompt introduction of retail competition.

Summarizing testimony to Administrative Law Judge Jeffrey Stockholm since NYSEG's settlement talks with the commission's staff broke off in late March, the filing -- and those of other participants in the case -- sets the stage for Stockholm's recommendation.
Participants have until June 23 to file replies to these post-hearing initial briefs.
Judge Stockholm told Reuters Monday there is no schedule for handing down his recommendation, which will be followed by another round of filings before the full commission rules.
Following the breakdown of talks, the utility filed what it called a "definitive settlement agreement," which the staff points out "is not an agreement."
Calling the NYSEG filing "ill-named," a filing from New York's Independent Power Producers and Enron Corp urged rejection saying "the proposed 'agreement' is neither definitive nor a settlement."
Several participants pointed out last week, as the latest filings were being prepared, that "no one has signed on" to the proposed "agreement."
The utility had made no announcement of its filing prior to late May rumors it had settled with the staff.
Those apparently arose when hearings were adjourned one day to allow discussions between the company, the staff and the Judge Stockholm, Mark Younger of Slater Consulting said.
And the staff filing notes that it agreed with NYSEG to extend the suspension of the utility's Year 2 rate so the issues could be resolved within the restructuring proceeding.

In response to questions, NYSEG issued a brief statement in early June saying it had filed a proposed settlement and detailing what it saw as the changes from its initial filing in late September 1996. Those points were"
-- All NYSEG customers would be able to choose their electricity supplier by August 1, 1999;
-- It would stabilize electric prices for five years;
-- Many large customers would see their prices reduced by 25 percent, while others could receive discounts for growth of increased electricity usage.
-- The company's current freeze of natural gas prices would be extended four more years through July 31, 2002.
-- NYSEG would forgo the $45.5 million electric price increase the Public Service Commission approved for the third and final year of the company's current electric rate settlement.
Spokeswoman Katherine Karlson has been unable since to discuss the proposal or even provide a copy of the document.
A copy provided by the commission showed it contained no mention of the second year rate increase, which has been suspended by the commission.
The staff's unwillingness to allow NYSE proceed with the second year of its settlement was rumored to be the reason settlement talks broke down in March.

Now the staff has recommended that the company receive neither the second or third year of the agreement, stating the emergence of competition "supersede(s) the prior rate increases adopted under a cost of service approach that no longer produces 'just and reasonable' rates."
The staff said the principles espoused in NYSEG March filing "are anti-competitive and faily utterly to meet the goals the commission identified" in calling for the proposal.
It joins the power producers and Enron in saying the only way to determine stranded costs would be an auction of NYSEG's fossil-fired generation assets.

Both the staff and Enron filings challenged NYSEG's unbundling proposal, which the Retail Council of New York said "fails to meaningfully unbundle rates in any regard" and "precludes" the development of retail competition.
((-- New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610.))
